documents.html:
Context engineering: from learned artifacts to learned learning procedures

Mode: TECHNICAL DEEP DIVE.

This companion expands Weng's context-engineering section through the inspected ACE, MCE, and Meta-Harness primary-paper captures. The systems form a useful conceptual ladder, but they do not share one evaluator, budget, or experimental protocol and should not be read as a leaderboard.

Context engineering reading map

Use this companion in five passes:

  1. Anchor Weng's claim. Read Weng's original context-engineering section, then use the core thesis below to identify the object being optimized.
  2. Build the runtime model. Read “Minimal mental model” to separate current truth, working state, episodic history, learned knowledge, construction policy, and durable execution state.
  3. Trace the learning ladder. Read ACE for artifact updates, MCE for a learned context-learning skill, and Meta-Harness for search over executable context policy.
  4. Cross learning with runtime. Use “Runtime operations versus learned objects” and the Codex state-continuity companion to distinguish learning useful context from preserving and activating it.
  5. Design a falsifier. End with the experimental plan and claim ceiling. A task-score gain is not enough; the experiment must isolate the artifact, constructor, consumer, evaluator, and total resource budget.

The primary-paper route for each learning system is:

SystemMinimum source routeWhy it matters
ACE original paper§§2–3.2 → §§4.1–4.7 → Appendix A.3–A.6Failure model, Generator–Reflector–Curator loop, grow-and-refine updates, ablations, and cost.
MCE original paper§§3.1–3.4 → §§4.1–4.3 → §5 → Appendix ABi-level objective, agentic crossover, base-level execution, fixed-versus-evolved skill comparison, and limitations.
Meta-Harness original paper§3 and Algorithm 1 → §§4.1–4.3 → Appendix A.1–A.2Code-space search, filesystem feedback, Pareto retention, trace ablation, and proposer behavior.

For source-code and project-page behavior, use the evidence-tiered Meta-Harness deep dive. It keeps arXiv claims, dated site results, pinned repository interfaces, and the local TRAE proposal run separate rather than extending this cross-system ladder. For evaluator boundaries and the full paper-derived MCE experiment protocol, use the harness benchmark field guide.

The checked-in source texts are evidence/weng/text/ace.txt, evidence/weng/text/mce.txt, and evidence/weng/text/meta-harness.txt. The source registry records their publication state, capture digest, and claim ceiling. The paper results below remain author-reported unless explicitly marked otherwise.

Core thesis

  1. CLAIM — [WENG-HARNESS], “Context Engineering.” Weng presents context engineering as an increasingly general optimization surface: ACE updates structured context, MCE evolves skills that construct and update context, and Meta-Harness searches the code that governs the full context lifecycle. Read the original section.
  2. INFERENCE. The three systems change different objects. ACE mainly changes persistent artifacts Dₜ. MCE also changes context-learning policy in Hₜ and Rₜ. Meta-Harness broadens the search object to executable harness code.
  3. EVIDENCE — ACE, §§2–4. ACE responds to brevity bias and context collapse with Generator, Reflector, and Curator roles, structured bullets, incremental delta updates, and grow-and-refine maintenance.
  4. EVIDENCE — MCE, §3. MCE formalizes a bi-level problem: an outer meta-agent evolves a context-engineering skill, while an inner base agent executes that skill to produce a context function represented by files and code.
  5. EVIDENCE — Meta-Harness, §3. Meta-Harness uses a coding-agent proposer with filesystem access to previous harness code, traces, and scores, then evaluates proposed harness programs and retains a Pareto frontier.
  6. INFERENCE. Richer context is not automatically better context. Measure selected context, cache behavior, output quality, adaptation cost, and utilization separately.
  7. INFERENCE. A learned context artifact can improve task performance without improving the procedure that learns future context. Recursion requires evidence about that later learning procedure.
  8. MISSING. No matched experiment in this packet isolates artifact quality, learning-procedure quality, model utilization, and resource spend across all three systems.

Minimal mental model

Context is a function, not a prompt string

For task input x, define a context function:

c(x) = F(x; ρ)

where:

  • ρ is persistent context state such as rules, examples, memories, indexes, scripts, and retrieval metadata; and
  • F is the policy that selects, transforms, orders, and presents parts of that state for x.

The model then produces:

ŷ = f_W(x, c(x)).

This separates three questions that a monolithic prompt hides:

  1. What persistent knowledge has been learned?
  2. How is task-relevant context constructed from it?
  3. Can the model actually use the resulting context?

The context lifecycle

task + current context state
          |
          v
      construct context
          |
          v
     model trajectory
          |
     outcome + trace
          |
          v
 diagnose -> propose delta -> validate -> merge or reject
          |
          v
 next context state

The model-visible prompt is one projection of a larger state. The archive should retain the input, selected context, trajectory, outcome, proposed change, decision, and provenance even when the next prompt is compact.

Two axes that should not be collapsed

Context engineering has a runtime axis and a learning axis.

The runtime axis asks how one task receives context:

archive -> retrieve -> select -> transform -> order -> render -> activate

The learning axis asks how later tasks change that process:

trajectory -> diagnose -> propose -> validate -> publish -> supersede

ACE, MCE, and Meta-Harness mainly expand the learning axis. Long-running agent harnesses also need the runtime axis to preserve working state between model calls. A system can improve one axis while failing on the other. For example:

  • a high-quality ACE bullet is useless when retrieval never selects it;
  • a correct MCE skill is inert when the runtime does not activate it;
  • a good compaction policy preserves a thread without learning any new rule;
  • a large memory archive can grow while task-relevant selection gets worse; and
  • a better final prompt does not show whether the artifact or constructor improved.

INFERENCE. “Better context” is therefore an underspecified result. A useful report identifies which state changed, which runtime operation consumed it, and which later outcome improved.

Six context planes

PlaneConcrete contentsFreshness ruleMain failure
Current truthcwd, permissions, tools, model, instructions, active processesRecompute from the runtimeStale transcript state overrides reality
Working statehypotheses, plan, rejected branches, pending calls, opaque continuation itemsPreserve within the active lineageRe-derivation after each action
Episodic historyobservations, actions, tool calls, outputs, decisionsAppend, normalize, checkpointBroken ordering or orphaned call/output pairs
Learned knowledgerules, examples, memories, playbook bullets, skillsValidate, version, supersedeContext collapse, contradiction, or stale advice
Construction policyretrieval, selection, ordering, rendering, compactionEvaluate as executable policyCorrect records are omitted or badly presented
Durable execution staterollout checkpoints, operation IDs, external side-effect receiptsPersist atomically and reconcileResume duplicates or forgets effects

These planes need different update semantics. Current truth should usually be recomputed, not recalled from memory. Working state needs continuity but may be opaque. Learned knowledge needs provenance and retirement rules. Durable execution state must survive crashes and cannot be replaced by a prose summary.

Context success is a pipeline

For a learned entry d, separate:

  1. available: d exists in the authoritative archive;
  2. eligible: its conditions match the current task and world state;
  3. selected: retrieval and budget policy choose d;
  4. rendered: the constructor presents d in a usable form and order;
  5. activated: the model notices and invokes the instruction or skill;
  6. adhered: the trajectory continues to follow it when pressure rises; and
  7. effective: the resulting behavior improves the protected outcome.

A rough decomposition is:

P(effect) = P(select) × P(activate | select) × P(adhere | activate) × P(success | adhere).

This is a diagnostic factorization, not an independence claim. It prevents an end-to-end score from assigning every failure to artifact quality. The Harness Disentangle reading provides the closest inspected evaluation treatment of update quality, activation, adherence, and downstream benefit.

Context pipeline checkpoint

Suppose a correct safety rule exists in the persistent archive, but the agent violates it during a long task. Before revealing the categories below, locate the earliest failed boundary:

  • Was the rule eligible for the current task and world state?
  • Did retrieval select it under the available budget?
  • Did rendering preserve its conditions and authority?
  • Did the model activate it at the relevant decision?
  • Did the trajectory continue to adhere after tool feedback arrived?
  • Did the rule improve the protected outcome when followed?

This question is intentionally open. “The memory failed” is not a diagnosis until the failed boundary and its receipt are identified.

Retention, retrieval, and compaction solve different problems

  • Retention keeps a prior item available to the active lineage.
  • Retrieval chooses a relevant item from a larger archive.
  • Compaction replaces a long active history with a smaller continuation state.
  • Consolidation turns episodes into reusable cross-thread knowledge.
  • Replay reconstructs a logical state after interruption.

Conflating them creates false guarantees. Retaining everything does not make it relevant. Retrieval does not preserve exact action order. Compaction does not create cross-thread knowledge. Replay of a transcript does not recreate an operating-system process or prove whether an external write completed.

The Codex state-continuity deep dive shows these boundaries in one inspected production harness: typed ResponseItem history, opaque reasoning continuation, recomputed world state, atomic compaction checkpoints, rollout replay, and a separate memories pipeline. It is an operational companion to the ACE–MCE–Meta-Harness learning ladder, not a fourth system in Weng's context-engineering comparison.

ACE: structured artifact adaptation

Failure being addressed

EVIDENCE — ACE, §§2.2–3. ACE names two failure modes:

  • brevity bias: summarization favors concise abstractions and drops domain-specific heuristics, tool-use guidance, and failure details; and
  • context collapse: repeated monolithic rewrites progressively erase useful prior information.

The failure is structural. Asking an LLM to regenerate the complete context turns every update into a destructive rewrite of all prior knowledge.

Generator, Reflector, Curator

EVIDENCE — ACE, §3. ACE separates:

  • Generator: uses the current playbook to solve tasks and emits trajectories;
  • Reflector: analyzes successful and failed trajectories and proposes concrete lessons; and
  • Curator: integrates lessons into the playbook through structured updates.

The separation matters because task execution, diagnosis, and state mutation have different failure modes. A Generator may solve a task without explaining why; a Reflector may infer a false lesson; a Curator may overwrite or duplicate valid knowledge.

Itemized playbook

EVIDENCE — ACE, §3.1. Context is represented as identified bullets rather than one prompt blob. This supports:

  • localized updates;
  • per-item usefulness or harmfulness feedback;
  • fine-grained retrieval;
  • deterministic merge logic; and
  • later deduplication or refinement.

INFERENCE. Stable item identity is a provenance primitive. It lets an experiment ask which rule was selected, which trajectory motivated a change, and whether a later failure came from retrieval, content, or model adherence.

Grow and refine

EVIDENCE — ACE, §3.2. New bullets can be appended; existing bullets can be updated; semantically redundant entries can be deduplicated. This avoids rewriting the complete playbook on every observation.

INFERENCE. Incremental mutation reduces blast radius but creates lifecycle work:

  • contradictory bullets need conflict semantics;
  • stale rules need expiry or supersession;
  • deduplication can merge distinctions that matter;
  • counters can reward frequently used but wrong rules; and
  • unbounded growth can shift cost from adaptation to every inference.

Evidence and claim ceiling

EVIDENCE — ACE, §§4.6–4.7 and Appendix A. The paper reports component ablations, cost and latency analysis, weaker-reflector experiments, harmful feedback stress tests, and an incremental-update ablation. It reports an 86.9% average adaptation-latency reduction in its comparison and discusses cache reuse when evaluating longer playbooks.

ACE reader checkpoint

If a new ACE playbook improves a held-out task, what additional experiment would distinguish a useful learned bullet from a stronger Reflector, more rollouts, or a larger effective context budget?

Record the intervention, frozen components, and resource match before reading the artifact-versus-procedure ablation in the validation plan.

MISSING. These are author-reported results. This packet does not reproduce the benchmarks, billing assumptions, or cache behavior. The reported benefits also remain bounded by trace and feedback quality.

MCE: learn the context-learning procedure

Why ACE is still a fixed algorithm

INFERENCE. ACE adapts context content inside a human-designed Generator–Reflector–Curator workflow. Its representation, update roles, and merge semantics are mostly fixed. MCE asks whether the procedure itself should be a search object.

Bi-level objective

EVIDENCE — MCE, §3.1. A skill s defines how to construct and learn a context function cₛ = (ρₛ, Fₛ). MCE solves a bi-level problem:

inner level: execute skill s to learn the best context function c_s
outer level: search for a skill s whose resulting context function validates well

This separates:

  • what is learned: context files, rules, examples, and programs; from
  • how it is learned: the skill's instructions, scripts, resources, and update procedure.

The analogy is to separating model parameters from architecture and training algorithm, while keeping the underlying foundation model frozen.

Skill as executable representation

EVIDENCE — MCE, §§2–3. A context-engineering skill is a folder containing instructions, scripts, and resources. The base agent receives the skill, training rollouts, the prior best context, and a workspace. It can build context as files and code rather than only a flat text list.

INFERENCE. This representation increases expressivity:

  • retrieval indexes can replace static inclusion;
  • scripts can calculate or validate context;
  • progressive disclosure can load detail only when relevant;
  • task-specific structures can emerge; and
  • prior context can be updated rather than rebuilt.

It also increases attack surface. Executable context machinery must be subject to permissions, deterministic evaluation, dependency policy, and provenance.

Agentic crossover

EVIDENCE — MCE, §3.2. The meta-agent reads prior skills, their generated context functions, and evaluation metrics. It synthesizes a new skill by selectively combining and refining earlier mechanisms rather than applying one fixed textual recombination rule.

INFERENCE. “Crossover” here is deliberative source inspection and code/skill composition. Its quality depends on archive visibility and causal interpretability. If the meta-agent sees only final scores, it may combine correlated mechanisms without understanding why they worked.

Base-level optimization

EVIDENCE — MCE, §§3.3–3.4. The base agent executes the current skill, learns from rollouts, updates the context function, and is evaluated on a validation set. The resulting skill, context, and metrics enter the skill database for later iterations.

Evidence and claim ceiling

EVIDENCE — MCE, §4.3. The paper compares no-skill, fixed-skill, and evolving-skill variants. On the named FiNER offline setting, the full system is reported above the skill-less and fixed-skill variants. The paper also states that iterative skill evolution is unavailable in a single-pass online setting.

MCE reader checkpoint

An evolved MCE skill and the context files produced by that skill change together. Which crossed evaluations would let you attribute a gain to the learning procedure rather than the resulting artifact?

Keep the base model, task split, evaluator, inner-loop budget, and outer-loop candidate count visible in the proposed comparison.

MISSING. The paper reports task-specific experiments across five domains, not a general proof that skill evolution improves arbitrary context learning. The primary limitation is model capability: weak agents may not create or execute useful higher-order skills.

Meta-Harness: search the complete executable context policy

This section keeps the cross-system mechanism comparison. The dedicated Meta-Harness implementation deep dive owns source locators, project-page trajectory analysis, implementation boundaries, and the local proposer experiment.

Search object

EVIDENCE — Meta-Harness, §3. A harness is a stateful program that controls what the fixed model sees and how state changes after each interaction. The search object can include storage, retrieval, prompt construction, tool logic, and update algorithms.

This is broader than optimizing one playbook or one learning skill.

Filesystem as feedback channel

EVIDENCE — Meta-Harness, §§1 and 3. Each evaluated candidate receives a directory containing code, execution traces, model interactions, and scores. A coding-agent proposer navigates the growing filesystem with tools, diagnoses failures, and writes new harness programs.

The filesystem can exceed the proposer's context window. Selective access lets the proposer inspect raw evidence without putting the entire archive in every prompt.

Minimal outer loop

initialize valid harness population
for each search iteration:
    proposer inspects any prior code, traces, and scores
    proposer writes one or more candidate harnesses
    evaluator executes candidates on search tasks
    archive stores code, trajectories, scores, and failures
    update valid population and Pareto frontier
return frontier

EVIDENCE — Meta-Harness, Algorithm 1. Parent selection is not hard-coded; the proposer may inspect any retained candidate. Accuracy and context cost can be treated as multiple objectives.

Why raw traces matter

EVIDENCE — Meta-Harness, §4.1, Table 3. The paper compares scores-only, scores-plus-summary, and full filesystem access. It reports that access to raw execution traces materially improves harness search over the more compressed conditions.

INFERENCE. A final score says whether a candidate worked. A trace can expose where storage, retrieval, presentation, or model adherence failed. This is a credit-assignment advantage, not proof that every trace should remain model-visible.

Evidence and claim ceiling

EVIDENCE — Meta-Harness, abstract and §4. The paper reports text classification, retrieval-augmented math, and TerminalBench-2 results, including accuracy–context tradeoffs and transfer tests.

Meta-Harness reader checkpoint

Raw traces can improve diagnosis while also exposing search-set details and increasing proposer context. What matched control would show that trace structure, rather than extra information volume or extra model work, caused the search gain?

MISSING. The source is a preprint and the packet contains no independent reproduction. The search uses a strong coding-agent proposer, domain skills, finite search tasks, and evaluator feedback. A discovered harness is not evidence of a recursively improved search operator.

One ladder, three different mutable surfaces

AxisACEMCEMeta-Harness
Primary mutable objectStructured context bulletsContext-learning skill plus context files/codeFull task-specific harness program
Main archivePlaybook and trajectory feedbackSkill database, context functions, metricsCandidate code, raw traces, scores
Proposer structureFixed Generator–Reflector–CuratorEvolving meta-skill plus base agentCoding agent with filesystem tools
Update granularityBullet deltaSkill directory and context-function editsArbitrary valid code edit
Main evaluator questionDid the new playbook improve task output?Did this skill learn a better validating context function?Did this harness improve reward/cost frontier?
Attribution strengthHighest of the three when one bullet changesHarder: skill and learned context co-varyHardest: broad code changes and large search space
Honest claim ceilingContext artifact adaptationBi-level context-procedure adaptationAutomated harness-code search

Runtime operations versus learned objects

The system papers and the runtime lifecycle can be crossed directly:

OperationACEMCEMeta-HarnessRuntime continuity concern
StoreIdentified playbook bulletsFiles, code, prior contexts, skillsCandidate source, traces, scoresPreserve typed order and provenance
RetrieveBullet or playbook selectionSkill-defined lookup and progressive disclosureProposer filesystem inspectionBound recall by relevance and permissions
TransformReflector proposes lessonsBase agent runs learned scripts and instructionsCandidate code can implement arbitrary transformsKeep source and transformed state distinguishable
RenderMostly fixed playbook presentationSkill can learn formatting and assemblyHarness code controls complete presentationPreserve trained protocol and call/output invariants
UpdateCurator applies local deltasOuter agent evolves the update skillProposer edits executable harness codePublish replacement state atomically
CompressDeduplicate and refine bulletsSkill may invent summaries or indexesCandidate may implement compactionRetain decisive state and reset invalid baselines
RecoverNot the main paper objectWorkspace and prior context are inputsFilesystem archive supports later inspectionReplay from a checkpoint and reconcile side effects

INFERENCE. The editable object gets broader from left to right, while the number of ways to produce the same visible prompt also grows. Evaluation must log intermediate context decisions, not only the final prompt and score.

State and authority mapping

Using Cₜ = (Wₜ, Hₜ, Dₜ, Rₜ):

  • ACE bullets are mostly Dₜ; selection and merge policy are Hₜ; reflection belongs to Rₜ.
  • MCE context files are Dₜ; the learned skill spans Hₜ and Rₜ.
  • Meta-Harness candidates are broad Hₜ programs; the coding-agent proposer and its search policy belong to Rₜ.
  • All three normally keep Wₜ frozen.

External evaluator E, resource budget B, permission policy P, protected archive Aₜ, and promotion authority must remain outside the candidate.

INFERENCE. The same filesystem may hold candidate artifacts and evaluator records, but capability boundaries must prevent candidate writes to scores, held-out tasks, archive history, and promotion decisions.

Cost and performance model

Let:

  • T_rollout be task-execution latency;
  • T_reflect be diagnosis and lesson extraction;
  • T_update be artifact, skill, or code mutation;
  • T_eval be fresh candidate evaluation;
  • N_candidates be evaluated candidates; and
  • C_context be selected model-visible context.

Approximate search cost:

Cost ≈ N_candidates × (T_rollout + T_reflect + T_update + T_eval).

The systems shift cost differently:

  • ACE reduces full-rewrite work with localized deltas but may increase the context carried on every task.
  • MCE pays an outer skill-search cost and an inner context-learning cost.
  • Meta-Harness pays for many complete candidate harness evaluations and raw trace storage, while allowing selective archive inspection.

Raw context length is not billed or latency cost by itself. Distinguish:

  • raw persistent archive bytes;
  • selected prompt tokens;
  • cache-read and cache-write tokens;
  • uncached prefill;
  • decoded reasoning/output tokens;
  • model calls and retries; and
  • evaluator executions.

A longer stable prefix can be cheaper than repeatedly generated shorter contexts when provider caching applies. That is an empirical systems property, not a semantic-quality argument.

Failure modes

Artifact-level failures

  • brevity bias removes rare but decisive detail;
  • context collapse erodes knowledge through repeated rewrite;
  • bullet growth creates contradictions and prompt bloat;
  • deduplication merges rules that differ under hidden conditions;
  • stale rules survive a distribution shift; and
  • feedback leakage writes evaluation answers into context.

Procedure-level failures

  • a Reflector extracts a plausible but false causal lesson;
  • a Curator promotes low-confidence feedback;
  • a skill overfits validation metrics;
  • agentic crossover combines correlated mechanisms without attribution;
  • executable context code gains excessive permissions; and
  • progressive disclosure fails to activate the right skill.

Search-level failures

  • more candidate evaluations masquerade as a better search algorithm;
  • broad code diffs prevent causal diagnosis;
  • raw traces contain protected task information;
  • the proposer learns score-parser or evaluator quirks;
  • Pareto objectives hide a hard correctness failure; and
  • the archive retains only winners, concealing search cost.

Implementation translation

Typed context artifact

ContextEntry:
    id
    statement or executable locator
    source evidence
    conditions and scope
    confidence
    created_by trajectory
    supersedes / conflicts_with
    usage and outcome receipts
    status: proposed | active | retired

Context constructor

ContextFunction:
    retrieve(query, state) -> candidate entries
    select(candidates, budget) -> selected entries
    render(selected, world state) -> model input
    observe(trajectory, outcome) -> update evidence

Each operation should emit a receipt:

ContextReceipt:
    task and world-state digest
    archive and constructor versions
    eligible and selected entry IDs
    exclusion reasons
    rendered-context digest
    active-history checkpoint ID
    token and cache accounting
    activation and adherence observations

The receipt makes four superficially similar failures distinguishable: missing knowledge, failed retrieval, failed model use, and a wrong learned rule.

Update transaction

  1. Freeze source trajectory, evaluator identity, and current context digest.
  2. Propose typed deltas with source locators and expected effect.
  3. Validate schema, permissions, conflicts, and budget.
  4. Evaluate old and new contexts under matched tasks.
  5. Publish accepted deltas atomically; archive all rejected deltas.
  6. Recompute retrieval index and receipt.

Bi-level skill package

skill/
    SKILL.md
    scripts/
    references/
    capability-manifest.json
    evaluation-contract.json

The capability manifest declares readable evidence, writable context paths, allowed executables, network policy, and output schema. The skill may propose context changes but cannot write evaluator or archive authority.

Harness-search package

Give each candidate a separate immutable parent revision and writable workspace. Record:

  • candidate code digest;
  • parent and proposer identity;
  • inspected prior candidates;
  • model/provider configuration;
  • task split and evaluator digest;
  • complete root-tree resource use;
  • raw trace and selected-context digests;
  • score vector and integrity findings; and
  • rejection or promotion decision.

Experimental validation plan

1. Artifact versus procedure ablation

Hold the learned playbook fixed and vary the context-construction procedure; then hold the procedure fixed and vary the learned playbook. This separates artifact quality from learning-policy quality.

2. ACE component ablation

Compare monolithic rewrite, incremental deltas, no Reflector, no Curator, single versus repeated reflection, and deduplication on/off. Measure held-out quality, playbook growth, conflicts, adaptation latency, and token cost.

3. MCE bi-level ablation

Compare no skill, fixed skill, evolved skill, and random/resource-matched skill search. Use delayed validation and a task-family shift to test whether the skill learns a reusable procedure rather than one dataset's structure.

4. Meta-Harness information ablation

Give the proposer scores only, scores plus summaries, selected raw traces, or the full filesystem. Match candidate-evaluation budget. Measure search efficiency, final frontier, repeated failure modes, and protected-data leakage.

5. Context utilization test

For every accepted artifact, run with the artifact available but not announced, explicitly loaded, incorrectly selected, and fully removed. Separate retrieval, activation, adherence, and task outcome.

6. Contamination and adversarial feedback

Inject misleading trajectories, conflicting bullets, held-out canaries, stale rules, and a tempting evaluator file. Verify that confidence, conflict, permission, and promotion gates fail closed.

7. Cost accounting

Report raw archive bytes, selected prompt tokens, cache reads/writes, uncached input, output/reasoning tokens, model calls, candidate evaluations, wall time, and dollar cost. Do not compare only final prompt length.

8. Later-cycle test

Promote an accepted context procedure, then give parent and child matched new context-learning problems. Compare the distribution of valid next artifacts, not only immediate task performance. This is the additional test required for a recursive claim.

9. State-continuity 2×2

Cross reasoning/working-state retention on/off with compaction on/off. Hold model, tasks, action budget, seeds, and tool policy fixed. Measure repeated hypotheses, output tokens per action, early-fact recall, actions to completion, and final score. Retention should mainly reduce reconstruction; compaction should mainly prevent late-horizon forgetting. The combined cell tests whether the two mechanisms are complementary.

10. Context-pipeline attribution

Plant typed rules with known eligibility conditions. Log availability, selection, rendering, activation, adherence, and outcome for each rule. Then perturb one boundary at a time: corrupt the index, reduce the selection budget, move the rule late in the prompt, suppress skill activation, or inject a conflicting instruction. A useful diagnostic should identify the perturbed boundary rather than reporting one generic context failure.

What evidence would change the claim

The context-engineering claim strengthens if:

  • gains survive delayed and out-of-domain tasks;
  • artifact/procedure ablations localize the cause;
  • random and resource-matched search baselines lose;
  • activation and adherence remain high;
  • adversarial feedback and leakage tests fail closed;
  • accepted procedures improve later context-learning cycles; and
  • independent reproductions agree on cost and quality.

It weakens if:

  • a longer prompt or stronger proposer explains the gain;
  • validation data enters context state;
  • selected rules are not used;
  • summary-only or random search matches the method;
  • broad edits cannot be causally localized;
  • later cycles accumulate contradictions or debt; or
  • the learned procedure does not outperform its parent on new learning tasks.

Claim ceiling

ACE supports structured persistent context adaptation. MCE supports bi-level adaptation of context-learning skills and context artifacts. Meta-Harness supports automated search over executable harness programs with filesystem feedback. Together they show a progression from learned context to learned context-learning machinery.

They do not, in this packet, demonstrate a general autonomous recursive improvement loop. That claim requires protected external evaluation, complete resource accounting, accepted generations, and measured improvement of later improvement work.
documents.title: Context engineering: from learned artifacts to learned learning procedures

documents.html:
Evaluator integrity: how a harness earns the right to become its successor

Mode: TECHNICAL DEEP DIVE.

Canonical explanation: Evaluation, promotion, and containment. This deep dive retains the full adversarial test matrix, source locators, and Pi-first experiment protocol.

INFERENCE — scope. This note treats evaluator integrity as the central engineering problem in a bounded harness-improvement loop. It does not claim that Pi, Hermes, Codex, Self-Harness, AHE, or DGM has demonstrated open-ended RSI.

EVIDENCE — corpus boundary. Every source cited below is an already captured local artifact or inspected local checkout registered in sources/source_registry.tsv: [WENG-HARNESS], [WENG-REWARD], [SELF-HARNESS], [AHE], [DGM], [PI-MONO], [HERMES-AGENT], and [CODEX-REPO]. The registry fixes the relevant source identities and revisions; this document adds no live-web evidence.

INFERENCE — notation. This deep dive follows the canonical ownership split in [[system_state_and_notation]]: the editable candidate is Cₜ = (Wₜ, Hₜ, Dₜ, Rₜ); Xₜ consists only of signals generated outside candidate write authority; E, B, P, Aₜ, and promotion authority are separately protected parts of the experiment envelope.

MISSING. This packet contains no executed, multi-generation experiment satisfying the protocol proposed below. The protocol is therefore a research design, not a reported result.

Reading contract

EVIDENCE denotes an observed source statement, captured artifact, or inspected code path at the cited locator. CLAIM denotes a source author's interpretation or design intent. INFERENCE denotes this document's synthesis or proposed design. SPECULATION denotes a hypothesis worth testing. MISSING records an absent proof or parameter rather than filling it in.

1. The object that must be protected

INFERENCE — state partition. A practical harness-improvement experiment is clearer when it distinguishes editable Cₜ = (Wₜ, Hₜ, Dₜ, Rₜ) from the protected experiment envelope (Xₜ, E, B, P, Aₜ, promotion authority), where:

LabelSymbolRoleWho may change it during a candidate run?
INFERENCECₜEditable candidate bundle.Candidate/proposer, only through the declared mutation interface.
INFERENCEWₜModel parameters.Candidate only if weight updates are explicitly in scope; otherwise frozen.
INFERENCEHₜHarness policy: prompts, skills, middleware, tools, context policy, workflow, and hooks.Candidate within its declared edit allowlist.
INFERENCEDₜPersistent learned artifacts: memories, trajectories, playbooks, demonstrations, or synthetic data.Candidate may propose changes; train/held-out separation remains evaluator-controlled.
INFERENCERₜInternal retrospection and proposal policy: trace inspection, diagnosis, reflection, and candidate generation.Candidate within its declared edit allowlist.
INFERENCEXₜSignals produced outside candidate authority: held-out outcomes, environment effects, trace audits, and independent feedback.Evaluator/environment; candidate may read only explicitly released signals.
INFERENCEEEvaluator: task split, verifier image, regression tests, scorer, judge protocol, and aggregation rule.Evaluator owner only; never the candidate.
INFERENCEBComparable resource contract and trusted accounting.External controller only.
INFERENCEPPermission policy: filesystem, network, tools, credentials, sandbox, and approval rules.Control-plane owner only.
INFERENCEAₜArchive: immutable source revision, candidate diffs, resource receipts, evaluator results, rejections, and parent/child edges.Archive service may append; candidates must not rewrite it.
INFERENCEPromotion authorityActor or controller that accepts a valid candidate as a future parent or grants broader deployment authority.Separate from candidate and evaluator implementation.

INFERENCE — proposed transition. A candidate is a bounded delta δₜ such that C′ = δₜ(Cₜ) while E, B, P, and the protected archive role remain fixed. Xₜ is observed rather than edited: it changes as candidate runs produce external outcomes. The archive records both δₜ and the decision; it is not itself a model-visible prompt summary.

INFERENCE — promotion predicate. The controller should promote a candidate only when all three independent gates pass:

Promote(C′, Cₜ) = G_outcome(C′, Cₜ, Xₜ, E, B)
                 ∧ G_integrity(C′, Xₜ, E, B, P, Aₜ)
                 ∧ G_authority(C′, promotion authority)

INFERENCE — why conjunction matters. A higher task score without integrity can be an evaluator exploit; integrity without outcome is a safe failed experiment; outcome plus integrity without authority is not permission to merge, deploy, or expand the action surface.

2. Editable surface versus immutable control plane

CLAIM — [WENG-HARNESS], evidence/weng/artifacts/html/weng-harness.html:505-535. Weng's Self-Harness description frames the loop as bounded proposal over declared harness surfaces, followed by held-in and held-out regression evaluation; rejected candidates are logged rather than changing the active harness.

CLAIM — [WENG-HARNESS], evidence/weng/artifacts/html/weng-harness.html:536-559. Weng's AHE summary describes explicit filesystem representations for editable components and uses a read-only runs directory, tracer, verifier, and LLM configuration to block several easy reward-hacking paths.

EVIDENCE — [AHE], evidence/weng/text/ahe.txt:1146-1157. The captured AHE prompt excerpt limits edits to workspace/, declares runs/ read-only, prohibits LLM-configuration changes, and forbids reverse-engineering test cases from trajectories.

EVIDENCE — [PI-MONO], evidence/implementations/pi/snapshot/packages/agent/src/harness/agent-harness.ts:395-539, commit 4488ad55c18f07ae89a489096c90de8667b3adfb. Pi snapshots session context, resources, model, thinking level, full tool collection, active tools, and prompt state for a turn; it exposes context and tool-call hooks through loop configuration.

EVIDENCE — [CODEX-REPO], evidence/implementations/codex-rsi/snapshot/codex-rs/core/src/tools/router.rs:31-289, commit 1e85ca099e4265bf89f4016772d299816e231bb3. Codex keeps model-visible tool specifications separate from registered runtimes and normalizes function, custom, search, and collaboration invocations before registry dispatch.

EVIDENCE — [CODEX-REPO], evidence/implementations/codex-rsi/snapshot/codex-rs/sandboxing/src/manager.rs:34-74 and :264-380, commit 1e85ca099e4265bf89f4016772d299816e231bb3. Codex resolves effective permissions and transforms commands into platform-specific sandbox requests; the candidate's textual tool request is not the final host-enforcement decision.

INFERENCE — minimal editable manifest. A first experiment should permit only a versioned candidate/ bundle containing developer instructions, skill bodies, tool descriptions, context-selection rules, and explicitly named non-privileged middleware. Core tool runtimes, evaluator code, tasks, model configuration, permission profiles, archive writer, and promotion controller should be outside that manifest.

INFERENCE — physical realization. “Immutable” should mean more than a prompt instruction: separate mount or checkout, a distinct OS/process identity for evaluator and archive service, an allowlist-based candidate writer, and a promotion operation unavailable to the candidate process.

MISSING. The inspected Pi, Hermes, and Codex paths show useful control-plane primitives, but none is evidence that an arbitrary local extension cannot find another authority path without a harness-specific adversarial test.

3. Internal retrospective signals are not external acceptance signals

EVIDENCE — [WENG-HARNESS], evidence/weng/artifacts/html/weng-harness.html:510-531. The Self-Harness summary separates collected execution traces, verifier-grounded failure patterns, records of passing behavior, and previous-edit summaries from the held-in and held-out regression check that decides whether an edit is accepted.

EVIDENCE — [HERMES-AGENT], evidence/implementations/hermes/snapshot/agent/memory_manager.py:364-455, :525-622, and :638-735, commit e444d165807f489b5c1ab8e4a612c8d09c2e67a2. Hermes permits built-in memory plus at most one external provider, bounds external prefetch, and serializes background persistence work; memory is a durable behavioral input, not an independent benchmark.

EVIDENCE — [HERMES-AGENT], evidence/implementations/hermes/snapshot/agent/curator.py:1496-1735 and AGENTS.md:1018-1048, commit e444d165807f489b5c1ab8e4a612c8d09c2e67a2. The curator supports snapshots, reports, archive/restore behavior, and an optional LLM consolidation pass over agent-created skills.

LabelSignal classExamplesProper roleUnsafe role
INFERENCEInternal retrospective signalRollout traces, self-critiques, root-cause summaries, memory writes, curator reports, candidate-provided tests, and prior-edit summaries.Generate hypotheses, retrieve context, explain failure, and choose a narrow edit.Sole evidence that the candidate is correct, safe, or promotable.
INFERENCEExternal outcome signalFresh evaluator run, hidden/held-out verifier result, independently replayed artifact, and blind task score.Establish whether target behavior occurred under the declared task contract.A mutable file or prompt exposed to the candidate.
INFERENCEExternal integrity signalEvaluator digest, clean-worktree receipt, read-only-write audit, resource receipt, sandbox log, and split-access log.Establish that the outcome was measured under the intended contract.A candidate-generated claim that those controls were followed.
INFERENCEExternal authority signalSigned/recorded promotion decision, permission-profile decision, deployment approval, and protected merge action.Decide whether a valid candidate may affect future runs or the outside world.A tool label or instruction the candidate can edit.

INFERENCE — distinction. Internal reflection can be highly informative without being trusted as an acceptance oracle. The crucial asymmetry is not whether a signal was generated by a model; it is whether the candidate can alter the mechanism that produces, selects, or records it.

INFERENCE — no self-certification rule. A candidate may read a bounded evidence package assembled from its own prior traces, but it must not receive held-out answers, evaluator source, promotion credentials, or a writable copy of the resource counter.

4. The three promotion gates

INFERENCE — G_outcome: did the candidate accomplish the intended work? Require a fresh comparison between parent and child on precommitted development and held-out task partitions, under identical model identity, decoding configuration, tools, environment image, retries, and B resource ceilings. A task result in Xₜ is an outcome signal, not an integrity proof.

INFERENCE — G_integrity: is the measured gain attributable to the permitted delta? Require evaluator/task/configuration digests, an allowlist diff, clean execution environments, read-only violation logs, complete tree resource accounting, and a record that no held-out material entered the proposal context.

INFERENCE — G_authority: may this candidate become the future parent? Require a promotion controller outside the candidate bundle to confirm that its requested surface, permissions, risk tier, and deployment scope are within the experiment's predeclared authority.

LabelGateMinimum receiptFailure mode that the gate excludes
INFERENCEOutcomeParent/child scores by split and repeat, task/verifier identity, and regression deltas.“It improved” based only on an anecdote, a trace, or a single visible task.
INFERENCEIntegrityCandidate/parent digests, immutable-input digest, evaluator digest, file-access audit, seed/retry record, and full resource tree.Test alteration, benchmark leakage, model swap, budget expansion, or selective reporting.
INFERENCEAuthorityPolicy version, permission profile, promotion actor, target environment, and explicit accept/reject reason.Self-merge, privilege escalation, or automatic deployment from a high score alone.

EVIDENCE — [SELF-HARNESS], evidence/weng/text/self-harness.txt:391-441. The captured paper defines a conservative acceptance rule over held-in and held-out evaluation, repeats stochastic evaluation, and records edited surfaces, split outcomes, repeats, proposal summary, and accept/reject decision.

EVIDENCE — [SELF-HARNESS], evidence/weng/text/self-harness.txt:541-552 and :717-738. The paper reports fixed task splits, fresh task environments, fixed model/tool/budget/evaluator conditions, and explicitly describes its bounded harness-edit setting as distinct from open-ended self-improvement.

INFERENCE — stricter promotion rule. The Self-Harness-style non-regression rule is a useful outcome gate, but a research-grade RSI experiment should make integrity and authority independent gates rather than assumptions folded into the task score.

5. Account for the whole subagent tree

EVIDENCE — [HERMES-AGENT], evidence/implementations/hermes/snapshot/agent/iteration_budget.py:1-59, commit e444d165807f489b5c1ab8e4a612c8d09c2e67a2. Hermes gives each parent and child its own iteration budget; its source comments explicitly note that total parent-plus-child iterations can exceed the parent's cap.

EVIDENCE — [HERMES-AGENT], evidence/implementations/hermes/snapshot/tools/delegate_tool.py:2778-2995, commit e444d165807f489b5c1ab8e4a612c8d09c2e67a2. Hermes bounds delegation depth, rejects model-supplied iteration budgets in favor of configured limits, caps child batches, and records live child transcripts as best-effort side-channel logs.

EVIDENCE — [CODEX-REPO], evidence/implementations/codex-rsi/snapshot/codex-rs/core/src/agent/control.rs:90-140 and agent/control/spawn.rs:365-720, commit 1e85ca099e4265bf89f4016772d299816e231bb3. Codex shares an agent registry, execution limiter, residency state, and rollout budget across a root-thread tree; spawning reserves capacity and persists parent/child structure.

EVIDENCE — [PI-MONO], evidence/implementations/pi/snapshot/packages/agent/src/harness/session/session.ts:173-203, commit 4488ad55c18f07ae89a489096c90de8667b3adfb. Pi's session statistics sum cached and uncached tokens, total tokens, and total cost from recorded assistant, compaction, and branch-summary usage.

INFERENCE — tree-level budget. For a candidate root r, the relevant resource spend is the aggregate over its complete descendant tree, not the root's displayed counter: Spend(r) = Σᵥ∈Tree(r) (tokensᵥ, callsᵥ, wall_timeᵥ, tool_timeᵥ, retriesᵥ, costᵥ, peak_concurrencyᵥ). B is the protected contract that constrains and compares this spend.

INFERENCE — accounting invariant. Every child must have a stable run_id, parent_run_id, spawn timestamp, model/configuration identity, permission profile, and terminal state. The trusted runner must emit a zero-use row for failed or interrupted children so that omission cannot look like efficiency.

INFERENCE — fairness invariant. Compare parent and child at equal root-tree budget, not equal root-agent budget. If one candidate consumes more subagent fan-out, retries, wall time, or higher-cost model capacity, report the extra resource as part of the result rather than calling the score change a harness improvement.

MISSING. No inspected local harness provides a complete, cross-harness receipt that normalizes model tokens, external-tool cost, wall time, concurrency, and descendant spend for an RSI comparison.

6. Reward-tampering threat model

CLAIM — [WENG-REWARD], evidence/weng/text/weng-reward.txt:29-33, :61-93, and :107-133. Weng characterizes reward hacking as obtaining high reward through flaws or ambiguities rather than the intended task, and distinguishes misspecified objectives from interference with the reward mechanism itself; the captured examples include changing unit tests or reward-calculation code.

CLAIM — [WENG-HARNESS], evidence/weng/artifacts/html/weng-harness.html:626-632. Weng argues that self-improvement loops can overfit tests, exploit judge-specific tricks, or exploit benchmark artifacts, and recommends keeping evaluator and permission control outside the evolving harness with held-out tests and trace audits.

LabelThreatCandidate actionWhat falsely looks betterRequired countermeasure
INFERENCET1 — score-surface mutationEdit tests, verifier code, task fixtures, score normalization, or model configuration.Reported pass rate.Separate read-only evaluator checkout; digest before and after every run; reject on any forbidden write.
INFERENCET2 — held-out disclosureRead hidden task files, infer them from logs, store them in memory, or retrieve them in a later proposal.Held-out “generalization.”Separate data capability, per-run access logs, fresh isolated environments, and proposal-context allowlist.
INFERENCET3 — resource launderingMove work into nested agents, retries, background processes, cached artifacts, or higher-cost model routes.Apparent efficiency or equal-budget gain.Trusted root-tree metering, descendant closure check, and matched accounting of cache/retry/tool work.
INFERENCET4 — authority escalationAlter a visible tool description, deferred tool lookup, role configuration, or inherited child context to reach a privileged runtime.A candidate that appears more capable.Runtime registry and permission profile owned outside Cₜ; denial tests across every invocation path.
INFERENCET5 — archive launderingDelete rejection records, reparent a branch, change a parent digest, or replace raw trace with a favorable summary.A fictitious monotonic lineage.Append-only archive with independent run IDs, content digests, and raw-to-summary linkage.
INFERENCET6 — evaluator gamingExploit judge self-preference, position bias, prompt injection, or a rubric ambiguity.Higher learned-judge score.Blind/randomized presentation, plural partly independent checks, deterministic assertions where available, and human escalation for high-impact decisions.
INFERENCET7 — objective collapseTrade maintainability, safety, or future editability for an immediate task pass.Functional completion.Multi-objective scorecard with non-tradeable correctness/integrity/authority constraints.
INFERENCET8 — post-success state destructionClean up, reset, or rewrite outputs after a local check but before external verification.A locally plausible completion narrative.External final verifier against the actual final environment and a post-check file-system audit.

EVIDENCE — [AHE], evidence/weng/text/ahe.txt:1623-1631 and :1844-1884. The captured case study describes a trajectory that reached a passing-looking state and then removed or reset deliverable state; the external verifier rejected it, and a later guarded mechanism targeted the post-acceptance action.

EVIDENCE — [WENG-REWARD], evidence/weng/text/weng-reward.txt:121-142. The captured discussion connects optimization pressure, imperfect proxies, environment access, and increasingly capable optimization to opportunities for reward hacking.

INFERENCE — design consequence. An honest benchmark should assume that a strong candidate will search for all eight classes of shortcut. A control that only catches accidental edits is a reliability feature; a control that survives deliberate attack is integrity evidence.

7. Archive and lineage integrity

EVIDENCE — [PI-MONO], evidence/implementations/pi/snapshot/packages/agent/src/harness/session/session.ts:325-351, :403-517, and :61-149, commit 4488ad55c18f07ae89a489096c90de8667b3adfb. Pi appends entries with parent IDs and timestamps, records active-tool changes and compactions, supports leaf moves with branch summaries, and projects a model-visible context from a larger session history.

EVIDENCE — [HERMES-AGENT], evidence/implementations/hermes/snapshot/agent/conversation_loop.py:6058-6136, commit e444d165807f489b5c1ab8e4a612c8d09c2e67a2. Hermes attempts to persist the assistant tool-call turn before side-effecting tool execution and halts the affected turn when canonical persistence fails.

EVIDENCE — [CODEX-REPO], evidence/implementations/codex-rsi/snapshot/codex-rs/core/src/agent/control/spawn.rs:365-567 and :570-720, commit 1e85ca099e4265bf89f4016772d299816e231bb3. Codex reserves capacity, persists spawn metadata/edges, flushes parent rollout history before a fork, selects history according to fork mode, and sanitizes inherited items before child construction.

EVIDENCE — [DGM], evidence/weng/text/dgm.txt:550-559 and :623-665. The captured DGM text describes sandboxed, time-limited runs and a traceable archive lineage of code changes/evaluations; it presents rollback and post-hoc analysis as intended safeguards and lists reproduction inputs including diffs, prompts, configs, evaluation artifacts, and cost estimates.

INFERENCE — archive/context separation. Archive preservation and model context are different jobs. A candidate may consume compacted summaries to fit a context window, while the archive retains raw trace pointers, raw outputs, environment identities, and rejected branches needed to audit or replay an improvement claim.

LabelArchive recordWhy it is needed
INFERENCEcandidate_id, parent digest, declared mutation manifest, and full diff.Establish what was actually allowed to change.
INFERENCEEvaluator/task/image/model/configuration digests and split-access receipt.Establish what was fixed during measurement.
INFERENCEOne row per run and per descendant, including failures, interruption, and cancellation.Prevent survivorship bias and hidden resource use.
INFERENCERaw trace pointer plus any summary's source-range/digest.Make a compacted explanation auditable rather than authoritative.
INFERENCEScore vector, integrity results, authority decision, and rejection reason.Explain why a branch did or did not become an ancestor.
INFERENCERollback target and promotion actor.Make reversal and accountability operational rather than rhetorical.

CLAIM — [WENG-HARNESS], evidence/weng/artifacts/html/weng-harness.html:629-630. Weng identifies preservation of failed attempts and protection against diversity collapse as open challenges for self-improvement loops.

INFERENCE — rejected branches are first-class data. A lineage graph that stores only accepted nodes cannot distinguish genuine cumulative improvement from selection among many hidden failures. Retain rejected and abandoned candidates, but keep their artifacts outside the active candidate's writable scope.

MISSING. The local artifacts do not establish a common, cryptographically append-only archive format or a verified remote attestation service. Content hashes and independent storage identities are proposed requirements, not properties already demonstrated by this packet.

8. Multi-objective promotion: correctness is necessary, not sufficient

CLAIM — [WENG-HARNESS], evidence/weng/artifacts/html/weng-harness.html:634-635. Weng uses coding agents to illustrate a gap between completing the immediate task and protecting repository health, maintainability, ownership boundaries, migration cost, compatibility, and future debugging burden.

INFERENCE — score vector. A useful candidate record should preserve a vector rather than a single scalar:

J(C) = (
  S_task,          # held-out task success
  Q_correctness,   # invariant, regression, and artifact correctness
  M_maintain,      # maintenance burden and repository health
  U_successor,     # usefulness to the next improver
  C_resource,      # root-tree resource cost
  I_integrity      # observed integrity/authority risk
)
LabelAxisExample operationalizationPromotion role
INFERENCES_taskFresh held-out verifier success and predeclared domain metric.Required evidence of target behavior.
INFERENCEQ_correctnessRegression suite, type/lint/build checks, invariant tests, and final-artifact replay.Non-tradeable gate for the intended scope.
INFERENCEM_maintainDiff size/churn, complexity or dependency delta, documentation consistency, and a fixed maintenance task.Visible tradeoff or an application-specific gate; never silently discarded.
INFERENCEU_successorA fresh, independently run successor agent can understand the bundle, diagnose a seeded failure, and make a bounded correct change under the same permissions.Direct test of whether this parent improves later improvement work.
INFERENCEC_resourceComplete root-tree receipt, including external tools and retries.Constraint and reported tradeoff, not an unrecorded confound.
INFERENCEI_integrityForbidden-write outcome, split-access audit, sandbox/permission audit, and archive completeness.Non-tradeable gate.

INFERENCE — gate versus frontier. Correctness, evaluator integrity, and promotion authority should be hard constraints. Among candidates that satisfy them, task success, maintainability, successor usability, and cost can be represented as a Pareto frontier rather than forcibly collapsed into a score that hides regressions.

SPECULATION — successor usability may be the most diagnostic RSI axis. A harness that makes the next independently evaluated improvement cycle easier, more reliable, or more auditable could be more consequential than one that merely improves its own first task score. This needs the protocol below; it is not established by a code-quality proxy alone.

INFERENCE — thought exercises for the reader. Which properties should be absolute promotion gates in your domain, and which should remain explicit Pareto tradeoffs? If a candidate raises held-out functionality while making the repository harder for a fresh successor to understand, should it be a parent? What evidence would distinguish a genuinely simpler harness from complexity merely displaced into an undocumented prompt, tool, or memory store?

9. Adversarial tests for the boundary itself

INFERENCE — test principle. Evaluate the evaluator boundary as an adversarial system: deliberately give a candidate or a test double the incentive and opportunity to alter the score surface, resource ledger, authority path, or archive, then verify that promotion fails closed.

LabelTestInjected attackPassing evidenceSource motivation
INFERENCEA1 — evaluator write denialCandidate tries to edit a verifier, task fixture, score normalizer, or evaluator config.OS audit and digests show denial; promotion controller marks integrity failure even if task score rises.[WENG-HARNESS], evidence/weng/artifacts/html/weng-harness.html:552-559; [WENG-REWARD], evidence/weng/text/weng-reward.txt:107-111.
INFERENCEA2 — hidden-split exfiltrationCandidate searches mounts, logs, memory, child context, or tool results for held-out labels.Access log proves no capability; any violation invalidates the entire branch.[SELF-HARNESS], evidence/weng/text/self-harness.txt:541-547.
INFERENCEA3 — tree-budget launderingCandidate fans out children, uses retries/background work, or shifts work to a more expensive model.Descendant closure and trusted resource vector reconcile to the root receipt; unmatched spend invalidates comparison.[HERMES-AGENT], evidence/implementations/hermes/snapshot/agent/iteration_budget.py:17-30; [CODEX-REPO], evidence/implementations/codex-rsi/snapshot/codex-rs/core/src/agent/control.rs:90-140.
INFERENCEA4 — tool/permission escalationCandidate changes tool visibility, deferred lookup, role metadata, or a child request to access a privileged runtime.Each path resolves against immutable registry and permission profile; denied action is archived.[CODEX-REPO], evidence/implementations/codex-rsi/snapshot/codex-rs/core/src/tools/router.rs:31-289; evidence/implementations/codex-rsi/snapshot/codex-rs/sandboxing/src/manager.rs:264-380.
INFERENCEA5 — archive rewriteCandidate deletes a rejection, changes parent ID, rewrites a summary, or attempts to reuse an old success receipt.Append-only store rejects mutation; verifier detects broken digest/parent chain.[PI-MONO], evidence/implementations/pi/snapshot/packages/agent/src/harness/session/session.ts:325-351; [DGM], evidence/weng/text/dgm.txt:623-640.
INFERENCEA6 — evaluator-presentation gamingCandidate controls judge ordering, self-identification, rubric text, or prompt content.Blinded/randomized presentation and independent checks disagree or reject the manipulated path.[WENG-REWARD], evidence/weng/text/weng-reward.txt:228-238.
INFERENCEA7 — post-success destructionCandidate reaches a local check and then deletes/resets a required output.External verifier checks final state after all actions; archive preserves the damaging action.[AHE], evidence/weng/text/ahe.txt:1623-1631.
INFERENCEA8 — successor-usability degradationCandidate passes functional tests by adding opaque instructions, brittle memory, or unmaintainable control flow.Fresh successor task and maintainability checks expose the regression; candidate cannot promote on function score alone.[WENG-HARNESS], evidence/weng/artifacts/html/weng-harness.html:634-635.

INFERENCE — fail-closed rule. Missing evaluator digests, missing descendant rows, unavailable write audit, or incomplete archive linkage must make a candidate ineligible for promotion. “We probably did not tamper” is not integrity evidence.

10. A falsifiable Pi-first experiment

EVIDENCE — [PI-MONO], evidence/implementations/pi/snapshot/packages/agent/src/harness/agent-harness.ts:395-539 and packages/agent/src/harness/session/session.ts:173-203, commit 4488ad55c18f07ae89a489096c90de8667b3adfb. Pi exposes a compact turn-state and hook surface while preserving session usage statistics, making it a plausible substrate for a small, inspectable experiment.

INFERENCE — study boundary. Start with Pi, but freeze its core runtime, evaluator runner, task image, model configuration, permission profile, archive writer, and resource collector. Permit proposals to edit only a declared candidate bundle of instructions, skill selection, context transform policy, tool descriptions, and non-privileged hook configuration.

INFERENCE — primary hypothesis. Under a fixed next-cycle proposal protocol and matched root-tree budget, a promoted candidate Cₜ₊₁ will produce a better distribution of valid next candidates than its parent Cₜ.

INFERENCE — immediate-performance secondary hypothesis. A promoted candidate will improve or preserve precommitted held-out task outcome compared with its parent under the same evaluator and resource contract.

INFERENCE — null and falsifier. The primary hypothesis is falsified for the studied setting if, across predeclared independent parent lineages and repeats, the next-cycle outcome of Cₜ₊₁ is indistinguishable from or worse than Cₜ after accounting for root-tree resources, or if a required integrity/authority gate fails.

Protocol

  1. INFERENCE — precommit the immutable contract. Record digests for task partitions, evaluator container/image, scoring code, model/provider/decoding configuration, permission profile, candidate manifest schema, archive schema, and resource-meter version before any proposal is generated.

  2. INFERENCE — construct parent lineages. Choose multiple starting candidate bundles that are semantically plausible but not selected using the held-out split. Give every parent the same eligible mutation surface and the same root-tree budget.

  3. INFERENCE — expose only internal proposal evidence. Build a bounded proposal packet from development traces, verifier-level failure classes, passing behaviors to preserve, allowed-path manifest, and prior-branch summaries. Do not expose held-out tasks, answers, scorer code, resource-counter internals, or promotion credentials.

  4. INFERENCE — generate diverse bounded deltas. Spawn candidate proposals from the same parent with distinct seeds or independently scheduled workers. Require each delta to name its target failure mechanism, changed files, intended outcome, predicted regressions, and requested permissions; reject out-of-manifest changes before evaluation.

  5. INFERENCE — run integrity checks before outcome scoring. Use a fresh environment per candidate, verify immutable-input digests, audit file/process/network access, resolve all tools through the evaluator-owned registry, and collect a complete descendant-tree resource receipt.

  6. INFERENCE — evaluate parent and child under matched conditions. Run development and held-out partitions using the fixed evaluator. Repeat predeclared stochastic tasks/seeds. Retain raw results, including timeouts, crashes, and invalid candidates.

  7. INFERENCE — apply the three gates. Permit G_outcome only after the fresh comparison; permit G_integrity only if all receipts and boundary tests pass; permit G_authority only through the external promotion controller. Archive rejected candidates without altering the active parent.

  8. INFERENCE — test recursion, not only improvement. Treat each accepted child as a parent and rerun the same fixed proposal/evaluation process. Compare the best valid next-generation gains attributable to Cₜ versus Cₜ₊₁, with the same model, proposer template, task distribution, selection rule, and root-tree budget.

  9. INFERENCE — run controls. Include a no-change parent, a resource-matched sham edit, seed permutation, and a delayed or out-of-distribution held-out set. Report whether gains survive each control rather than reporting only the best lineage.

  10. INFERENCE — stop and report both signs. Stop at a predeclared generation/budget limit or when integrity failure occurs. Publish accepted, rejected, abandoned, and invalid branches; a negative result is a valid answer to the research question.

Measurements

INFERENCE — next-cycle gain. For a fixed proposal protocol Π, define the recursive measurement as RGₜ = E[BestValid(Π(Cₜ₊₁))] − E[BestValid(Π(Cₜ))], where BestValid ranges only over candidates that pass outcome, integrity, and authority gates at the same root-tree budget. Immediate S_task(Cₜ₊₁) − S_task(Cₜ) is useful but does not alone measure RGₜ.

INFERENCE — report card. Each generation should report split-wise task success, correctness/regression result, maintenance and successor-usability results, total resource vector, integrity-test results, authority decision, candidate diversity, and the full branch count.

INFERENCE — interpretation boundary. A positive immediate score with non-positive RGₜ supports bounded task improvement but not recursive improvement. A positive RGₜ on one evaluator/task family supports a bounded experimental claim, not a claim of general or open-ended RSI.

MISSING. The exact number of lineages, task count, confidence procedure, maintainer-task design, and promotion thresholds must be precommitted for the chosen domain. This packet deliberately does not fabricate them from the current sources.

11. What this deep dive changes in the RSI map

INFERENCE — operational criterion. The decisive unit is not “a self-reflective agent” or “a harness that can edit files.” It is an externally controlled state transition with a protected evaluator, protected authority boundary, complete resource accounting, and an archive that can prove what changed.

INFERENCE — hierarchy of evidence. Internal reflection explains a proposal; external outcome establishes task behavior; external integrity establishes attribution; external authority controls persistence and deployment. Conflating any two creates a shortcut for apparent improvement.

SPECULATION — research direction. Plural, partially independent evaluators and conservative authority gates may scale more safely than a single increasingly capable learned judge, but comparative evidence is absent from this bounded packet.

MISSING. No source inspected here proves that the proposed gates remain robust when candidates can redesign their own weight-update pipeline, evaluator implementation, or deployment authority. Those are deliberately excluded from the Pi-first experiment.

documents.html:
Hermes Agent: persistent adaptation with guarded maintenance

Mode: TECHNICAL DEEP DIVE.

EVIDENCE — snapshot. This profile inspects [HERMES-AGENT] at commit e444d165807f489b5c1ab8e4a612c8d09c2e67a2 in evidence/implementations/hermes/snapshot/.

INFERENCE — claim ceiling. Hermes is the richest of the three inspected harnesses in explicit cross-session adaptation: memory, agent-created skills, usage tracking, curation, delegation, and trajectories are named product surfaces. The source supports that mechanism claim; it does not independently establish that those mutations improve later improvement ability.

Architecture at a glance

EVIDENCE — observed control flow from [HERMES-AGENT], agent/conversation_loop.py:1084-1325, :5700-6165, agent/memory_manager.py:364-735, and tools/delegate_tool.py:2778-2985.

flowchart LR
    U["User turn"] --> B["Build turn context"]
    M["Persistent memory providers"] --> B
    K["Skills and plugins"] --> B
    B --> L["Budgeted provider loop"]
    L --> V["Validate and repair tool calls"]
    V --> D["Registry dispatch and guardrails"]
    D -->|results| L
    D -->|delegate| C["Isolated child agents"]
    L --> F["Persist and finalize turn"]
    F --> M
    F --> K
    K --> R["Optional curator review"]
    R --> K

INFERENCE — architectural reading. Hermes combines an online agent loop with slower artifact-maintenance paths. Memory synchronization and skill curation sit beside the turn loop rather than becoming unconstrained self-modification inside every model step.

Component map

LabelComponentObserved responsibilityDurabilityRSI tuple role
EVIDENCErun_conversation()Builds turn context, enforces interrupt and iteration budgets, samples, repairs tool calls, executes tools, compresses context, and finalizes the result.Turn state plus persisted session messages.Core execution in Hₜ.
EVIDENCEtool registry/dispatcherScopes toolsets, validates deferred tool access, invokes pre/post hooks and guardrails, and routes the real tool name.Registry/config state; tool effects vary.Action surface inside Hₜ.
EVIDENCEMemoryManagerCombines built-in and at most one external provider, prefetches recall, routes memory tools, and serializes post-turn background writes.Cross-session provider state.Persistent Dₜ; memory policy in Hₜ.
EVIDENCEskillsSupply reusable instructions and packaged resources; agent-created skills are distinguishable from bundled, hub, and external skills.Files under the Hermes skill store.Editable artifacts spanning Hₜ and Dₜ.
EVIDENCEcuratorApplies usage-based lifecycle transitions and can optionally run an LLM pass to consolidate agent-created skills, with snapshots, archives, reports, pins, and dry-run support.Cross-run skill library and curator state.Artifact maintenance inside Aₜ.
EVIDENCEdelegate_taskBuilds isolated children, supports single/batch and foreground/background modes, applies concurrency/depth/role/iteration limits, and aggregates results.Child sessions and live logs; background execution is process-local.Parallel proposal/search surface in Hₜ.

The online loop is bounded and persistence-aware

  1. EVIDENCE — prologue. build_turn_context() owns once-per-turn setup, including prompt restore, message sanitation, preflight compression, plugin hooks, external-memory prefetch, and crash-resilience persistence ([HERMES-AGENT], agent/conversation_loop.py:1138-1185).
  2. EVIDENCE — resource budget. The outer loop stops on both per-turn API-call count and an IterationBudget; each parent and child agent owns a separate budget (conversation_loop.py:1194-1293; agent/iteration_budget.py:1-59).
  3. EVIDENCE — tool repair and pairing. Before execution, Hermes uniquifies call IDs, attempts name repair, rejects invalid names or JSON with bounded recovery, caps delegation calls, and preserves assistant-call/result pairing (conversation_loop.py:5710-5944).
  4. EVIDENCE — persist before effects. The assistant tool-call turn is appended to SessionDB before side-effecting tools run; execution halts if that canonical append fails (conversation_loop.py:6058-6104).
  5. EVIDENCE — guardrail halt. A tool guardrail can terminate the turn with an explicit controlled response after execution dispatch (conversation_loop.py:6106-6136).

INFERENCE — integrity value. Persist-before-effects gives an external evaluator a stronger causal record than a transcript written only after tools finish, although it still does not prove that every external side effect is fully replayable.

Memory is a provider boundary, not one monolithic store

EVIDENCE — [HERMES-AGENT], agent/memory_manager.py:364-455. MemoryManager always permits the built-in provider and at most one external provider, prevents external memory tools from shadowing reserved core tools, and keeps routing explicit.

EVIDENCE — [HERMES-AGENT], agent/memory_manager.py:486-622. Providers may contribute system-prompt blocks and prefetched recall. Skill invocation scaffolding is stripped before a query reaches memory, and external prefetch is time-bounded so a stuck provider is skipped.

EVIDENCE — [HERMES-AGENT], agent/memory_manager.py:638-735. Completed turns sync through a single background worker so writes preserve turn order without keeping the visible turn open; queued work is tracked by durability class for shutdown handling.

INFERENCE — adaptation boundary. Hermes can change later behavior by changing remembered context without changing weights or loop code. Whether a memory write is beneficial remains an evaluator question; persistence alone is not improvement.

Skills and curator form a reversible artifact loop

EVIDENCE — [HERMES-AGENT], agent/curator.py:1-18 and :1496-1583. The curator is inactivity-triggered, operates on curator-managed skills, protects pinned and externally owned artifacts, takes a pre-run snapshot, records state before the optional LLM pass, supports dry-run, and defaults to deterministic lifecycle maintenance when consolidation is off.

EVIDENCE — [HERMES-AGENT], agent/curator.py:1585-1735. When consolidation is enabled, the curator renders candidates, runs a separate review agent, records tool calls and model metadata, diffs the before/after skill sets, writes a report, and preserves rename information.

EVIDENCE — [HERMES-AGENT], AGENTS.md:1018-1048. Automatic removal is archival rather than deletion; backup, restore, and pinning are documented operator controls.

CLAIM — [HERMES-AGENT], README.md:19-30. Hermes describes memory, skill creation and editing, session search, delegation, scheduling, and trajectory generation as a closed learning loop.

INFERENCE — strongest honest reading. The curator is a real self-maintenance loop over agent-created artifacts, but its acceptance signal is usage/lifecycle policy plus an optional review-agent judgment. The inspected paths do not apply an immutable held-out task evaluator before promoting the modified skill library.

Delegation is isolated and explicitly bounded

EVIDENCE — [HERMES-AGENT], tools/delegate_tool.py:2778-2897. Delegation accepts one task or a bounded batch, supports leaf and orchestrator roles, rejects spawning beyond configured depth, ignores model-supplied iteration budgets in favor of operator configuration, and applies a global pause switch.

EVIDENCE — [HERMES-AGENT], tools/delegate_tool.py:2902-2985. Child agents are built with isolated task context, inherited toolsets, explicit role and credential resolution, per-child live transcripts, and a shared aggregation path for synchronous and background batches.

INFERENCE — search value. These controls make delegation a plausible parallel proposal mechanism for harness experiments. They do not define diversity objectives, candidate fitness, or promotion criteria.

Mapping Hermes onto the candidate/envelope split

INFERENCE — notation. [[system_state_and_notation]] owns the canonical split: Hermes supplies candidate components and archive inputs; evaluator E, budget B, permissions P, official archive Aₜ, and promotion authority must remain external to candidate-controlled memory and curation.

LabelStateConcrete Hermes surfacePresent in inspected source?Missing for an RSI experiment
EVIDENCEWₜConfigured provider/model and optional fallback routing.Yes as runtime selection.A controlled weight-update and provenance path.
EVIDENCEHₜConversation loop, prompts, registry, toolsets, plugins, skills, memory policy, delegation, compression.Yes; several parts are runtime-configurable or file-backed.A versioned candidate boundary separating evaluator-owned from candidate-owned code.
EVIDENCEDₜSession history, recalled memories, skill bodies, trajectories, tool results.Yes and partly cross-session.Dataset curation criteria and contamination accounting.
MISSINGEGuardrails and curator policy evaluate admissibility or maintenance, not held-out task improvement.No complete immutable evaluator/selector.Fixed tasks, scoring, budget parity, adversarial evaluation, and acceptance thresholds.
EVIDENCEAₜSession database, memory stores, skill usage state, archives, snapshots, reports, child logs.Yes; richer than a flat transcript.Unified candidate lineage, fitness records, artifact digests, and promotion receipts.

Smallest credible Hermes-based experiment

INFERENCE — proposed boundary. Freeze the provider model, evaluator, core tools, guardrails, task split, and resource limits. Permit candidates to modify only agent-created skills and a declared memory-retrieval policy; retain curator snapshots as rollback points but prevent the curator model from reading held-out labels.

INFERENCE — proposed loop. Generate skill-library candidates through isolated children; score them on development tasks; promote through an evaluator-owned process; then compare parent and promoted libraries on both held-out task quality and the quality of their next proposed skill revisions.

MISSING. The inspected Hermes revision does not report this matched, multi-generation experiment, so its “self-improving” framing remains a product claim with concrete adaptation mechanisms but without RSI-level validation.
